status: Four reviewed source-fit authoring resolutions; A1.3 remains a proposal with its multiple actual Indigenous-community then/now qualifier unresolved.

inheritedReviewedPackets.role: Actual bounded First Nations, Métis, Inuit and settler life facts and source limits; five core cases plus the bounded Assiniboine role supplement.
inheritedReviewedPackets.limits: The repertoire supplies particular knowledge, not the whole historical inquiry or every source clause.

inheritedReviewedPackets.role: Particular regional agreements, parties, commitments, consequences and continuing relationship evidence.
inheritedReviewedPackets.limits: Toronto/Ajetance, Haldimand and Wiikwemkoong are different peoples/places. No invented wampum exchange or universal treaty terms.

inheritedReviewedPackets.role: Dated actual current Nipissing work/roads/business and Niagara visitor-service facts, used only for supported present-day comparisons.
inheritedReviewedPackets.limits: Provider accounts are not employment shares or every family’s daily experience.

facts: The Nation identifies current road, water and wastewater/public-works responsibilities and a business park serving commercial/light-industrial activity. These are verified selected present-day work and service roles.
limits: Compare the described work with a specific historical case; do not imply that every Anishinaabe community or every household has identical work or that older practices disappeared.

facts: The reviewed letters describe particular home work, sugar-making, local transport and practical challenges in an Upper Canada settler setting.
limits: An attributed settler observer’s account, not a neutral description of every woman, child, class or Indigenous neighbour. Exclude racist judgments rather than presenting them as facts.

facts: The reviewed sources place the Elgin/Buxton foundation in1849 and describe building and schooling work by1849–1850. The community provided a specific response to racial exclusion and the search for secure settlement.
limits: The church source has its own institutional perspective. Do not import the1859school or later buildings into1850, or claim racism ended.

facts: The previously reviewed1805/1808Anishinaabe case, Michipicoten1827–28Métis-family accounts and bounded Inuvialuit shelter/food/learning account support selected specific life and setting comparisons.
limits: Retain each case’s actual dates, place, observer and continuity qualification. Later museum collections or1850saccounts are not automatically evidence of every1780practice.

actions: Build a comparison matrix from the reviewed Anishinaabe, Métis, Inuvialuit, Buxton and Traill packets. Select several genuinely documented everyday aspects, including shelter/food, work and family learning/contributions. Record each actual place, date and source beside the fact. An absent fact remains unknown, not evidence that a community lacked that activity.

Explain supported similarities and differences between selected communities, referring to their setting and circumstances. Preserve differences within and between peoples; a named case is not every First Nation, every Métis community or all Inuit.

Use the bounded Assiniboine role supplement only with its exact1808–09place/date and outsider-observer limit if comparing the named men/women/children tasks. Do not project historical divisions as what people ought to do today.
period-life-comparison.positive: Accurate case-specific comparison over more than one ordinary-life dimension, including selected First Nations, Métis, Inuit and settler examples.
nearMiss: Repeats one generic account for all communities.
Fills an unrecorded activity with a stereotype.
period-life-comparison.transfer: Classify a new attributed fact from a studied source into the matrix and explain which comparison it changes.

actions: Choose documented historical work/learning roles and challenges from the period packets, including an Indigenous case. Compare them with verified current Nipissing public-works/business roles and a clearly supplied contemporary school/home scenario. Distinguish actual public case facts from an invented present-day teaching scenario.

For example, compare obtaining and transporting food/materials in a studied period case with a described contemporary water/road service role; explain both a continuing need and a changed duty or challenge. Compare a documented child’s historical contribution with the supplied modern school/helper situation without assuming every child has the same home.

Describe what the sources support about changing tools/services and continuing cooperation or environmental demands. Do not infer that contemporary Indigenous people are frozen in the past, that older knowledge has vanished or that all change is improvement.
roles-and-challenges-then-now.positive: Compares specific duties and challenges then and now, including a selected Indigenous community contribution, with continuity and change supported separately.
nearMiss: Says all people long ago had one job and all people today another.
Calls a supplied fictional present-day account an observed fact about every pupil.
roles-and-challenges-then-now.transfer: Compare a different documented historical role with a new supplied present-day situation and justify a continuing need and a changed circumstance.

actions: For studied Anishinaabe/Métis trading and Inuvialuit seasonal living cases, explain source-supported connections among waterways, access to food/materials, movement, exchange and settlement. For Traill/Buxton, explain supported farming, access/transport, housing, schooling or community-support considerations. Include both physical setting and goods/services rather than treating settlement as caused by climate alone.

Use the actual period place references to locate these cases broadly; do not substitute a modern reserve or membership boundary for a historical settlement area. Compare at least two supported development factors and how a selected feature or service helped people meet a need.

Use the existing land-use claim to distinguish housing, food/water use, work/services and transport purposes. Environmental knowledge is supplied accurately; no new soil calculation, navigation or climate mechanism is required.
settlement-setting-and-support.positive: Explains particular, evidence-supported development factors in varied communities including Indigenous cases, and connects physical features and available goods/services with community life.
nearMiss: Assumes all settlements developed for the same reason.
Treats proximity to water alone as proof of a particular trade or industry.
settlement-setting-and-support.transfer: Given a new short verified case, identify which stated setting/support factors explain its development and what remains unproven.

actions: Describe at least two supported challenges in different studied communities, including at least one Indigenous case: access to food/materials/transport and isolation in the reviewed ordinary-life accounts; displacement or land pressure in the actual studied treaty histories; racial exclusion and the1849–1850Buxton response.

Keep each problem in its actual period and place. A later residential-school policy belongs to the separate A1.2timeline, not to every1780–1850case. Explain what is known and where the source only records one observer’s experience.
period-challenges.positive: Describes more than one real period challenge with accurate case attribution and an Indigenous case.
nearMiss: Moves a twentieth-century school date into1800.
Converts one observer’s judgment into an entire people’s characteristic.
period-challenges.transfer: Decide whether a newly supplied dated source supports a period challenge claim and identify the fact that warrants the decision.

actions: Compare particular cooperation and conflict/unequal-power relationships between different studied communities: documented Anishinaabe/Métis–trading-post exchange and shared practical contributions; British/Six Nations or Great Lakes alliance relationships from the treaty packet; and settler pressure/displacement or disagreements over commitments in Toronto/Ajetance accounts.

Identify the actual parties, shared activity or contested interest and a supported consequence. A relationship can involve both cooperation and conflict across time; an agreement’s existence does not prove all dealings were fair or all obligations fulfilled.

Use respectful, attributed descriptions. Distinguish ordinary contemporary cooperation skills from knowledge of what the historical communities actually did; no new interpersonal-conflict training topic is needed.
community-relationships.positive: Describes source-backed intercommunity cooperation and conflict in specific period cases and explains why the labels fit rather than relying on nationality stereotypes.
nearMiss: Labels every treaty as proof of harmonious relations.
Calls all contact conflict or assumes every Indigenous nation held one view.
community-relationships.transfer: Evaluate a fresh short account of interaction between two studied communities, separating what it establishes from an unsupported generalization.

boundaries: Seven reviewed component pairs extend exact existing CA8–9 contexts. The additional proposed A1.3 pair is not authored; no new band, claim, guide or edge.

The new historical knowledge cards retain their complete repertoire and assessment. These tasks establish source-fit authoring for the named clauses; a component success does not infer all historical mastery.

A1/A2/A3major goals, later-policy A1.2, Canadian identity A1.4, historical maps/relocations A3.1, settler locations A3.2, different settlement impacts A3.5 and the historical inquiry remain separately unresolved in the current ledger.
Original protocols are untested teaching designs. No learner record, performance certification or classroom efficacy claim is made.

pendingCodes.A1.3: Provide at least two actual Indigenous community cases across historical and contemporary roles AND challenges, using source-supported contemporary facts. A fictional modern scenario may supplement but cannot stand for an unsourced actual community.
